title: Exponential law for compact-test mapping spaces of k-spaces
statement: For a topological space $T$, let $kT$ be the same set with topology in which $U$ is open exactly when $a^{-1}(U)$ is open for every continuous map $a:C\to T$ from a compact Hausdorff space $C$. Call $T$ a k-space when this topology equals its given topology. Let $X,Y,Z$ be k-spaces. On the set $Z^Y$ of all functions from $Y$ to $Z$, put the topology generated by $S(a,U)=\{f:f(a(C))\subseteq U\}$, where $a:C\to Y$ is continuous, $C$ is compact Hausdorff, and $U\subseteq Z$ is open. Give the subset $C(Y,Z)\subseteq Z^Y$ of continuous maps its induced subspace topology [def-kun-subspace-topology]; thus its subbasis consists of the intersections $S(a,U)\cap C(Y,Z)$. Then currying $h\mapsto(x\mapsto(y\mapsto h(x,y)))$ induces a bijection $\operatorname{Cont}(k(X\times Y),Z)\cong\operatorname{Cont}(X,kC(Y,Z))$, natural in $X,Y,Z$. All products before applying $k$ have the ordinary product topology. No Hausdorff or local compactness hypothesis is imposed on $X,Y,Z$.

source.place: WANTED: Hovey, Model Categories, Proposition 2.4.22(5), printed p.58 (PDF p.68); read online 2026-10-17. The source refers to Lewis, Appendix, for the proof; no Stacks tag.

proof.text: Write $M=C(Y,Z)$ with the subspace topology in the statement [def-kun-subspace-topology]. We first unpack the definition of $k$. The identity $kT\to T$ is continuous, and any continuous $a:C\to T$ with $C$ compact Hausdorff is continuous as a map to $kT$, since the inverse image of every $k$-open set is open by definition. Consequently a function $v:kT\to W$ is continuous if and only if $v\circ a:C\to W$ is continuous for every such ordinary test map into $T$. The forward implication uses the lift of $a$, and the reverse says precisely that $v^{-1}(U)$ is $k$-open for each open $U\subseteq W$. If $A$ is a k-space and $f:A\to T$ is continuous, then $f:A\to kT$ is continuous: for a $k$-open $V\subseteq T$, test $f^{-1}(V)$ against each $b:C\to A$, obtaining the open set $(fb)^{-1}(V)$. Tests into $T$ and $kT$ therefore coincide, so $k(kT)=kT$.

proof.text: For any two compact Hausdorff test spaces $C,D$, their ordinary product $C\times D$ is compact by [lem-weil-pbc-tychonoff-product-quasi-compact], specialized to a two-element index set. It is Hausdorff: two unequal pairs differ in one coordinate, and inverse images under that projection of disjoint neighbourhoods separate them. Thus every ordinary continuous map $C\times D\to T$ lifts to $kT$ by step 1. Also, each compact Hausdorff $D$ is locally compact in the neighbourhood-basis sense: its whole space is a compact neighbourhood of each point, so [lem-coef-hausdorff-compact-neighborhood-basis] applies. These assertions include empty test spaces.

source.place: Definition 2.4.21 and Proposition 2.4.22(5), printed p.58 (PDF page 68); compact-test proof supplied by the worker, using the cited Mathlib leaves.

proof.text: Let $h:k(X\times Y)\to Z$ be continuous. For fixed $x\in X$, the function $h_x(y)=h(x,y)$ is continuous on $Y$: for every compact Hausdorff test $a:D\to Y$, the map $d\mapsto(x,a(d))$ is continuous into $X\times Y$, hence into its $k$-ification by step 1, so $h_xa$ is continuous; the definition that $Y$ is a k-space now proves continuity of $h_x$. Thus $g(x)=h_x$ belongs to $M$. Fix a test $b:C\to X$ and a subbasic set $S(a,U)\cap M$, where $a:D\to Y$ is a compact Hausdorff test. By step 2, $(c,d)\mapsto(b(c),a(d))$ lifts continuously to $k(X\times Y)$. Apply the continuous-transpose clause of [lem-coef-compact-open-currying] to $H(c,d)=h(b(c),a(d))$. It gives a continuous map $C\to\operatorname{Cont}(D,Z)$ with the ordinary compact-open topology, since $D$ is locally compact by step 2. The inverse image of the subbasic open $[D,U]$ under this transpose is exactly $(gb)^{-1}(S(a,U)\cap M)$. Hence $gb:C\to M$ is continuous for every test $b$.

source.place: Definition 2.4.21 and Proposition 2.4.22(5), printed p.58 (PDF page 68); compact-test proof supplied by the worker, using the cited Mathlib leaves.

proof.text: Since $X$ is a k-space, the last assertion of step 3 proves that $g:X\to M$ is continuous: the preimage of any open of $M$ is open after every compact Hausdorff test into $X$. The lifting calculation in step 1 then proves that the same function $g:X\to kM$ is continuous. This constructs currying on the stated set of continuous maps.

source.place: Definition 2.4.21 and Proposition 2.4.22(5), printed p.58 (PDF page 68); compact-test proof supplied by the worker, using the cited Mathlib leaves.

proof.text: Fix a compact Hausdorff $D$ and a continuous $q:D\to Y$. Restriction $R_q:M\to\operatorname{Cont}(D,Z)$, $R_q(f)=f\circ q$, is continuous for the ordinary compact-open topology on the target. Indeed, if $L\subseteq D$ is compact, its subspace is compact by the definition of compactness for a subset, and is Hausdorff by restricting disjoint neighbourhoods from $D$. The restriction $q|_L:L\to Y$ is therefore an allowed test, and $R_q^{-1}([L,U])=S(q|_L,U)\cap M$, which is open by the subbasis defining $M$. The induced topology [def-kun-subspace-topology] ensures that these are precisely opens in the continuous-map subset.

source.place: Definition 2.4.21 and Proposition 2.4.22(5), printed p.58 (PDF page 68); compact-test proof supplied by the worker, using the cited Mathlib leaves.

proof.text: Conversely let $g:X\to kM$ be continuous and set $h(x,y)=g(x)(y)$. For any compact Hausdorff test $r:D\to X\times Y$ into the ordinary product, write $p=\operatorname{pr}_Xr$ and $q=\operatorname{pr}_Yr$. Then $D\xrightarrow{p}X\xrightarrow{g}kM\to M\xrightarrow{R_q}\operatorname{Cont}(D,Z)$ is continuous by step 5 and the identity $kM\to M$. The compact-neighbourhood-basis lemma applied to $D$ makes $D$ locally compact. Thus the continuous-evaluation clause of [lem-coef-compact-open-currying], with $A=K=D$, gives the continuous function $F:D\times D\to Z$, $F(d,e)=g(p(d))(q(e))$. Pulling back along the continuous diagonal $d\mapsto(d,d)$ gives $h\circ r$. Step 1 now proves that $h:k(X\times Y)\to Z$ is continuous. Local compactness has been used only for $D$, never for $X$ or $Y$.

source.place: Definition 2.4.21 and Proposition 2.4.22(5), printed p.58 (PDF page 68); compact-test proof supplied by the worker, using the cited Mathlib leaves.

proof.text: The formulas in steps 3 and 6 are inverse pointwise: $h^\sharp(x)(y)=h(x,y)$ and $g^\flat(x,y)=g(x)(y)$. They give the required bijection, including the empty-space cases. For naturality let $u:X^{\prime}\to X$, $v:Y^{\prime}\to Y$, and $w:Z\to Z^{\prime}$ be continuous maps of k-spaces. The ordinary map $M\to C(Y^{\prime},Z^{\prime})$, $f\mapsto w\circ f\circ v$, is continuous because the inverse image of $S(a,U)$ is $S(v\circ a,w^{-1}(U))$. The $k$-lifting calculation of step 1 makes the same map continuous between the $k$-ified mapping spaces; it likewise gives continuity of the induced map $k(X^{\prime}\times Y^{\prime})\to k(X\times Y)$. Both orders of currying and these pre/postcompositions evaluate at $(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})$ to $w(h(u(x^{\prime}),v(y^{\prime})))$, proving naturality in all three variables.
